transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-01-18
Start: 14:00 PT
Duration: ~47 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Jonah Park (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Redwood Marketing), Aaron Levy (Quantos co-founder), Sofia Marin (Quantos Head of Product), Diego Ramos (Quantos ML Eng)
Recording link: https://app.redwood.example/recordings/ff-20270118-quantos (placeholder)

Auto-generated summary (may be imperfect): Quantos migrated from self-hosted inference to Redwood Private to reduce tail latency and total cost; they use a mixed strategy (hosted for dev, private for production), ran a canary, and saw ~35% token-cost reduction with average p95 latency improvements. They discuss model rollouts, evals, and a story about a tough onboarding spike at launch.

----- Transcript -----
[00:00:00] Priya: Hey everyone, welcome to the Quantos founders roundtable. I'm Priya from Redwood marketing — thanks for joining. We might cut this into a 20 minute episode but uh we're recording the whole thing for notes. Aaron, you want to kick us off with a short intro of Quantos?
[00:00:18] Aaron: Yeah sure, hey thanks Priya, hi Maya, Jonah. So Quantos builds a real-time intelligence layer for e-commerce — product recommendations, creative personalization. We were a little bit early to large-scale inference, we had our own infra, which became, um, fairly expensive and fragile.
[00:00:35] Sofia: And hi Diego — I mean we went from a small on-prem cluster to multi-cloud GPUs, a lot of operational debt.
[00:00:42] Maya: Love that paper trail, yeah. For listeners: Quantos started with self-hosted, then evaluated several vendors, ran a proof-of-concept with Redwood, and ended up on Redwood Private. We'll ask about why and the numbers.
[00:00:58] Jonah: Quick tech note before we go deep — Diego, if you can remind folks of the baseline hardware and model families you were running before Redwood, that'll help.
[00:01:06] Diego: Sure. Mostly A100 40GB nodes, some T4s for lighter workloads. Models were a mix: fine-tuned Llama derivatives and a few OSS narrow models for rerank. We were managing our own KV cache layer, uh, which we called the "k versus cache" in internal notes — ha — that of course caused some issues at scale.
[00:01:27] Priya: (laughs) k versus cache, noted.
[00:01:30] Aaron: Yeah, the cache mis-syncs were a real pain. So when Redwood came in, the thing that sold us was the ability to do consistent serving across environments and the rollout tooling.
[00:01:41] Sofia: And the console — the visibility was night and day compared to dashboards we cobbled together.
[00:01:47] Maya: Can you share the rough before/after on cost and latency? Even ballpark is helpful for listeners.
[00:01:54] Aaron: Ballpark — before, our per-million-token cost was... honestly it fluctuated a lot, but around $X, and after tuning with Redwood batching and cache features we saw roughly a 30–40% reduction. P95 latency improved from ~420ms to 250ms for our standard user workflow. Those numbers depend on load, of course.
[00:02:13] Jonah: To add — you also moved some traffic to quantized variants right? Diego, you did the quantiza— quanizat... sorry — effort there. How did that go?
[00:02:23] Diego: Yeah, we tried int8 quant on a copy of the model. Redwood's runtime accommodated that pretty smoothly. We had a couple of artifacts — small accuracy hits on certain prompt families — but the Redwood Optimize recommendations helped identify which endpoints to keep full precision and which to quant. That mixed strategy is what gave the biggest savings.
[00:02:44] Priya: Awesome. Let's step back for a sec — the decision to go private vs hosted — listeners will have tradeoff questions — what tipped you?
[00:02:52] Aaron: Two things. One, data residency and some enterprise customers asking for VPC options. Two, predictable latency at peak — our Black Friday style spikes. Hosted would have been fine for dev and early prod, but for our largest accounts we wanted the control.
[00:03:06] Sofia: Also our legal team wanted customer data to be fully in our VPC, and Redwood's private deployment + KMS integration fit.
[00:03:13] Maya: Nice. Any hiccups during the migration? People like stories about surprised bugs.
[00:03:18] Aaron: The funniest was our canary — we thought we were ready, but a small prompt family that triggered heavy rerank loads blew up KV hit ratios. We had to pause the canary, add a prefix cache on Redwood for that route, and re-run. The Redwood SE team — Jonah — helped us instrument it quickly.
[00:03:39] Jonah: Yep, we added a route policy with a higher cache TTL and a fallback variant. That reduced upstream calls and stabilized the canary.
[00:03:47] Diego: Also a small note: our team had some misconceptions about continuous batching — we initially worried it would add latency for single-user flows. The Redwood docs helped, but in practice the batching is workload-aware and didn't hurt our p50s.
[00:04:01] Priya: That feels like a great nugget for the episode — tradeoffs people actually have.
[00:04:05] Aaron: Totally. Another quick point — regression testing. We run prompt sets and Redwood's eval hooks let us gate new model rollouts. We caught a subtle hallucination drift once on a fine-tune; because we had the eval set, the canary failed and we rolled back.
[00:04:22] Sofia: QA saved us. The integration with our CI was straightforward, we just call the Redwood rollout API as part of the pipeline.
[00:04:29] Maya: listeners might ask about SLOs and SLAs — how did you approach defining them?
[00:04:34] Aaron: We defined two SLOs: p95 latency under 400ms for the personalization route, and availability 99.9 for dedicated routes. Redwood's dedicated capacity made that predictable.
[00:04:46] Priya: Were there any surprises on billing or metering?
[00:04:50] Sofia: The transparency was good — token-level breakdowns helped us map cost to features. We did learn that long context conversations inflate bills, so we started trimming system prompts and using prefix caching more aggressively.
[00:05:03] Jonah: Quick practical question for Diego — what's your stack for observability and where did you instrument Redwood traces?
[00:05:09] Diego: We forward traces to our Datadog setup; Redwood's trace hooks let us tag by customer_id and model_version which made top-down debugging much easier.
[00:05:19] Priya: Cool. Switching gears — product use cases, what's live today that's interesting?
[00:05:24] Aaron: Two big ones: real-time personalized descriptions and a creative assistant that suggests ad text. The creative assistant runs a hybrid flow — short prompts on a cheaper variant and longer generative drafts on higher-capacity models.
[00:05:37] Sofia: The creative assistant is also where we leaned into function-calling to get structured output to our downstream A/B system. We had a bit of a hiccup where function args weren't validated in earlier runs, but Redwood's streaming and function support smoothed that out.
[00:05:50] Aaron: Also interesting is reranking — instead of shipping raw candidate sets we now do an on-edge rerank with a small model which saved user-perceived latency.
[00:05:58] Priya: On the marketing side, do you have any quick lines or quotes that we can use in the case study?
[00:06:03] Aaron: Sure: "Redwood made inference operational — predictable performance at scale and the playbook to make it repeatable." If you need shorter: "Predictable inference, lower cost — shipped."
[00:06:14] Priya: Perfect. We'll send those for approval.
[00:06:17] Maya: A couple of listener questions we sometimes get: how much engineering time did you reallocate after moving to Redwood?
[00:06:23] Sofia: We estimate about 1.5 FTEs freed from infra toil — security and SRE hours dropped a lot because Redwood handled autoscaling and the incident runbooks cut our mean time to recovery.
[00:06:36] Diego: Plus we could focus more on prompt engineering and eval development.
[00:06:40] Jonah: Did you run benchmarks during the POC — any files we should link?
[00:06:44] Aaron: Yes, we have a bench spreadsheet and a short benchmark video. We'll share links. (Note: link placeholder in show notes).
[00:06:52] Priya: Great to include. Okay, let's do a quick lightning round — favorite Redwood feature?
[00:06:57] Diego: Rollouts API.
[00:06:59] Sofia: Console traces.
[00:07:01] Aaron: Predictable dedicated capacity.
[00:07:03] Maya: Nice. Listener: any advice for teams thinking about migration?
[00:07:08] Aaron: Start with a small but representative canary set, define evals early, and instrument cache metrics. Also budget for a two-week stabilization window.
[00:07:19] Sofia: Don't assume quantization is plug-and-play; validate on your specific prompts.
[00:07:24] Maya: Good advice.
[00:07:26] Priya: We're at the half-hour mark — we have a few audience Qs we prepped: one around compliance — SOC2 / KMS — did you have to change your contract to accommodate enterprise customers?
[00:07:36] Aaron: We used Redwood's standard enterprise addendum and KMS integration; the biggest change was data retention policy alignment. The Redwood compliance package helped speed up legal review.
[00:07:47] Priya: Nice. Another quick question: any roadmap asks you want Redwood to prioritize?
[00:07:52] Diego: A more granular cost-explorer per-route would be useful — like per-customer token slice for internal chargeback.
[00:07:59] Aaron: And native support for our in-house feature flags to route a % of traffic to new variants via Redwood policy would be great.
[00:08:07] Maya: Noted — we actually have an internal RFC on per-route costing, I'll link it.
[00:08:13] Priya: We're getting close to the end — last rapid-fire: what surprised you most about working with Redwood?
[00:08:18] Sofia: The speed of the onboarding playbook — we got a working canary in under two weeks.
[00:08:22] Aaron: The amount of control without adding ops was surprising in a good way.
[00:08:26] Priya: Amazing. Okay, let's do a short recap and next steps. Maya?
[00:08:31] Maya: Recap: we'll produce a 20–25 minute edited episode, include two soundbites from Aaron, and a short technical segment with Diego. Action items: Maya to share dashboard screenshots, Priya to produce the episode, Aaron to approve quotes and logo.
[00:08:48] Priya: And we'll share the bench artifacts and a short show notes doc. Diego, thanks for the technical color — we might use a 90-second clip for the dev newsletter.
[00:08:58] Diego: Happy to.
[00:09:00] Aaron: Thanks everyone.
[00:09:02] Priya: We'll stop recording in a sec — after this we'll just do a quick off-camera chat about conference speaking slots.

[00:09:12] -- Off-record ad-lib (not for publish) --
[00:09:12] Aaron: Quick note— we might want a joint workshop at Shoptalk in March.
[00:09:18] Maya: Let's sync calendars after we wrap.

[00:47:00] [end of call]

Notes on transcript quality: automated transcription had a few mis-heard acronyms (KV cache -> "k versus cache") and some punctuation errors. The marketing team will manually edit for the published transcript.
